name: Corpus callosum
summary: The great commissure of about 200 million axons joining homologous areas of the two hemispheres, arching over the lateral ventricles in the floor of the interhemispheric fissure. Its rostrum and genu connect the frontal lobes, the body the motor and parietal regions, and the splenium the occipital and temporal lobes. It lets the hemispheres share information, so its interruption (surgery, infarction, tumor, demyelination) causes disconnection syndromes: alexia without agraphia when the splenium is cut with the left occipital cortex, left-hand apraxia and agraphia when the anterior body is cut. Lesions of the callosum are a hallmark of multiple sclerosis, diffuse axonal injury and butterfly glioma.

anatomy.location: Midline, above the septum pellucidum and fornix and below the cingulate gyrus, from the rostrum beneath the genu in front to the splenium above the pineal region behind; its fibers spread as the radiations into the centrum semiovale and form the forceps minor and major at either end.

subdivisions.name: Body
subdivisions.note: premotor, motor, somatosensory and parietal connections

subdivisions.name: Isthmus
subdivisions.note: pre- and postcentral and auditory connections

subdivisions.name: Splenium
subdivisions.note: posterior parietal, temporal and occipital connections (forceps major)

function: Interhemispheric transfer of sensory, motor and cognitive information; coordination of bimanual movements; transfer of visual information from the right hemisphere to left-hemisphere language areas.

bestView.label: rostrum, genu, body and splenium on the midline
body of the callosum forming the roof of the lateral ventricles

imaging.normalAppearance: The bright white arch on midline sagittal T1; thinning of the body or splenium suggests chronic white matter disease or hydrocephalus, and callosal lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson's fingers) on sagittal FLAIR are characteriztic of multiple sclerosis.

pathology.finding: Ovoid FLAIR-bright lesions at the callososeptal interface and perpendicular to the callosum on sagittal FLAIR.
Microhemorrhages in the splenium and body on SWI after rotational trauma; associated with poor outcome.
Enhancing mass crossing the callosum into both hemispheres; lymphoma is homogeneously enhancing and restricts diffusion.
Transient oval restriction in the splenium with encephalitis, antiepileptic withdrawal or metabolic disturbance; reversible.
Absent callosum with parallel lateral ventricles (racing car sign), colpocephaly and radially oriented medial gyri.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal FLAIR and T1; SWI for trauma; DWI

lesionEffects.mechanism: Splenium plus left occipital lobe: the seeing right hemisphere cannot reach the left language cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Left-hand apraxia and agraphia, left tactile anomia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Anterior body: left hemisphere language cannot reach the right motor cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Alien hand syndrome and intermanual conflict
lesionEffects.mechanism: Anterior callosal disconnection with medial frontal involvement
Slowly growing lesions and congenital agenesis are compensated

examination: Name objects placed in the left hand with eyes closed
Write with the left hand and imitate gestures with each hand
Read words presented briefly in the left visual field
Observe for a hand acting on its own
pearls: Disconnection syndromes are easily missed: test each hand and each visual field separately
A lesion crossing the callosum is a glioblastoma, lymphoma or demyelination, not a metastasis
